title: Starship Reaches Orbit, Then Explodes After Splashdown
summary:
SpaceX's Starship rocket has finally reached orbit — but the milestone came with a few tense moments and an explosive ending.

On September 28, Starship launched on its 14th flight, the company's first attempt to send the rocket into orbit. Shortly after liftoff, one of its 33 engines failed. The mission team spent several tense minutes deciding whether to continue. Eventually, the call came: 'Go for orbit.' A short booster burn nudged Starship into orbit, where it circled Earth at a highest point of 170 miles (275 kilometers).

Starship then deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites, designed to boost the speed and reliability of SpaceX's satellite internet network. But because of the engine loss, SpaceX decided not to leave the rocket in space for the full 10-hour mission. Instead, it splashed down in the Pacific Ocean after 3 hours and 8 minutes — and then exploded with a fiery bang.

An explosive landing was always expected for Starship, and there were cheers during that part of the livestream. But SpaceX would likely have preferred to keep the rocket intact, as it did on Flight 13.

Before this launch, Starship had only flown suborbitally. Reaching orbit represents the 'next phase' toward becoming a fully reusable rocket, according to SpaceX. The company has experienced multiple setbacks with Starship: the seventh and eighth test flights exploded, the ninth fell short, and a Starship exploded on the launchpad during a routine test before the 10th mission. However, the 10th flight in August 2025 was successful, and the 11th was clean. The last two flights, in March and July 2026, had successful launches and controlled landings but experienced booster problems.

The stakes are high. NASA wants to use a moon-landing variant of Starship to ferry astronauts to the lunar surface during the Artemis IV mission in early 2028. With rival Blue Origin lagging behind, the Artemis program's success could be tied to Starship's. Today's engine issue leaves key questions about whether SpaceX can meet that tight deadline.
why_it_matters: Reaching orbit is a real step toward a fully reusable rocket, but the engine failure and explosion raise questions about whether Starship will be reliable enough for NASA's Artemis IV crewed Moon landing in early 2028, with few competing options available.

background_read: SpaceX (a private aerospace company founded by Elon Musk) is now the world's busiest launch provider, and its Falcon 9 rockets land their boosters and fly again — a trick the company pioneered that made reaching orbit far cheaper.

Starship is SpaceX's next-generation vehicle, designed to be fully reusable and to carry both satellites and people; the company deliberately pushes early prototypes to failure during testing, so explosions there are treated as data rather than disasters.
Starlink (SpaceX's growing network of internet satellites in low Earth orbit) is the company's main source of revenue and depends on regular launches to keep expanding.
NASA's Artemis program (named after the twin sister of Apollo in Greek mythology) aims to put astronauts back on the Moon for the first time since the Apollo missions more than fifty years ago.

Blue Origin (the space company founded by Amazon's Jeff Bezos) is developing its own rockets and a lunar lander, but has flown far fewer missions than SpaceX, leaving NASA with limited alternatives for a crewed Moon landing.

perspectives.description: Starship reached orbit for the first time and deployed 26 satellites, showing the vehicle can do the job it was built for and moving SpaceX closer to a fully reusable rocket.
An engine failed on the way up, the mission was cut from ten hours to three, and the rocket exploded at splashdown; with flights 7 and 8 lost earlier, NASA's reliance on Starship looks risky.
SpaceX has always learned by flying hardware and accepting losses, a faster and cheaper approach than traditional aerospace testing but one that keeps failure in the headlines.
The Artemis IV deadline is tight and Blue Origin is behind, so SpaceX must fix engine and booster problems quickly, or NASA may need to rethink how it lands astronauts on the Moon.
